To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the number of alleles at a locus is not a sufficient condition for polymorphism, (2) spatial variation may allow polymorphism to be maintained at a single locus, (3) temporal variation allows the stable coexistence of equilibrium configurations that are not stable under spatial variation, and (4) polymorphism may be more stable with temporal than spatial variation among environments.

(1) spatial variation allows the simultaneous maintenance of equilibria which cannot be simultaneously maintained under total panmixa; (2) temporal variation allows the maintenance of equilibra which cannot be maintained under total panmixture; and (3) the principle that polymorphism will be more readily maintained with soft selection than with hard selection is invalid

the following conditions are necessary for polymorphism to be stable: (1) the number of alleles at the locus is large enough to permit the simultaneous stability of more than one equilibrium configuration; (2) the variation among selection regimes is not too great; and (3) the variation is not too spatially structured.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of variable environments upon polymorphism at lociof the type considered by Lewontin and Hubby (1966) and Kimura and Ohta (1971).
the effect of variation among selection regimes on polymorphism.
the effects of variable environments on the stability and maintenance of polymorphism at a locus with several alleles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

spatial variation among selection regimes is a more powerful cause of polymorphism than temporal variation, but that temporal variation allows stable polymorphism which is impossible with spatial variation.

polymorphism at a single locus is most readily maintained with spatial variation among selection regimes and that polymorphism at several loci is most readily maintained when the environments vary over time.
the effects of spatial and temporal variation are qualitatively the same, but that the quantitative effects of the two types of variation may be quite different.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of variable environments are more subtle and more varied than has been suggested by the analyses of two alleles at a locus.
polymorphism is maintained by spatial variation among environments when selection is sufficiently soft.
spatial variation among selection regimes allows a greater variety of polymorphisms to be stable than does temporal variation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of variable environments is to alter the stability properties of equilibria and to allow the simultaneous stability of equilibria which are stable in isolation.
the effects of spatial and temporal variation are not easily separable, as they are in the two-allele models.
the effect of variable environments is more complicated with multiple alleles than with two alleles.
